snip.t: Kidney (glomerulus & tubules): Filtration pressure, sodium handling, tubuloglomerular feedback — Hypertensive nephrosclerosis and secondary causes (renal artery stenosis, glomerulonephritis) alter this feedback, perpetuating hypertension
Look‑alike conditions – hypertensive nephrosclerosis, HIV‑associated nephropathy, sickle‑cell nephropathy; differentiate by proteinuria pattern (DKD: albuminuria > 300 mg/g, often with retinopathy).
Uncontrolled hypertension can exacerbate the disease progression by causing arteriolar nephrosclerosis and by increasing the hyperfiltration injury.

qs.q: What pathological change defines nephrosclerosis in relation to systemic blood pressure?
o: Deposition of immune complexes within the glomerular basement membrane
Hardening of renal arterioles caused by and causing hypertension
Complete obliteration of the main renal artery by fibromuscular dysplasia
Destruction of red blood cells via microangiopathic thrombi
qs.e: Nephrosclerosis is defined as the hardening of renal arterioles, which is both caused by and causes hypertension. Immune complex deposition characterizes glomerulonephritis rather than primary nephrosclerosis.

qs.q: A 57-year-old man has had blood pressure measurements in the range of 160/95 to 180/110 mm Hg for many years. He has taken no medications. A renal scan reveals kidneys of normal size for age. These findings with benign nephrosclerosis are most likely to occur with which of the following vascular changes?
qs.e: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is a feature of long-standing hypertension and is part of benign nephrosclerosis which may go on for many years with no complications. The small arterioles are thickened with pink (hyaline) proteinaceous deposits.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Nephrosclerosis is the hardening and scarring of small renal arteries, driven mainly by chronic hypertension. It leads to ischemic damage, progressive kidney failure, and a vicious cycle that worsens blood pressure.

sections.p: Nephrosclerosis refers to fibrous thickening of renal arterioles, causing ischemic injury to the cortex and medulla. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by imaging and biopsy when feasible.

t.b: Is the kidney filtering properly? Elevated indicates reduced function.
Detects proteinuria or hematuria, suggesting glomerular involvement.
Assesses arterial flow; absent or reduced flow supports arteriolar disease.
Confirms arteriolar thickening and fibrosis when imaging is inconclusive.

sections.p: Staging follows the KDIGO chronic kidney disease stages, correlating with eGFR and proteinuria. Early stages show mild hypertension; advanced stages present with oliguria and electrolyte imbalance.

The primary driver is long‑standing hypertension. Other contributors include diabetes, aging, and systemic vasculitis. In low‑resource settings, infections such as HIV and malaria can exacerbate vascular injury.

t.b: Identifies uncontrolled hypertension as the root cause.
Detects diabetes contributing to vascular damage.

sections.p: Patients often have asymptomatic hypertension, gradual decline in renal function, and may develop edema or anemia. Sudden worsening can occur with acute tubular necrosis or superimposed infection.
Use readily available tests; when unavailable, rely on clinical judgment and basic labs.

t.b: Measures kidney filtration; rising levels indicate worsening function.
Detects hyperkalemia or hyponatremia from impaired excretion.
Shows small, echogenic kidneys typical of chronic disease.

sections.p: Rapid loss of urine output, severe hyperkalemia, or uncontrolled hypertension are emergencies. Complications include heart failure, electrolyte disturbances, and progression to end‑stage kidney disease.
Control blood pressure with ACE inhibitors or ARBs, avoid nephrotoxic drugs, and manage anemia and mineral bone disorder. Treat underlying causes such as diabetes.

t.b: Does it lower intraglomerular pressure? Yes, it protects the kidney.
Does it reduce edema? Yes, it removes excess fluid.

sections.p: Regular monitoring of blood pressure, kidney function, and proteinuria is essential. Lifestyle changes and early treatment of hypertension prevent progression.
Renal artery stenosis presents similarly but is a focal narrowing; acute tubular necrosis shows sudden creatinine rise without chronic changes.
Serum creatinine may remain normal until late stages; proteinuria can be transient in infections.

faq.a: Early stages can be stabilized with blood pressure control, but fibrosis is irreversible.

faq.q: Does it always cause kidney failure?
faq.a: Not always; many patients remain stable for years with good BP control.

faq.q: What is the role of ACE inhibitors?
faq.a: They lower intraglomerular pressure, slowing progression and reducing proteinuria.
